Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Eight years ago, Tane, a man of Pacific descent, was driving his sedan on a rain-slicked interstate when emergency lights forced him to pull over. What began as a routine stop fractured when an officer moved with rigid urgency, stepping directly into Tane’s personal space and pressing his face against the open window to demand identification. The officer’s heavy breathing and the sudden, deafening crack of his two-way radio shattered Tane’s sense of safety. Hours of bureaucratic delay followed before the misunderstanding cleared, leaving Tane trembling in his idling car. The encounter had been defined by an aggressive stranger invading his intimate space, a protracted, anxious wait, and a sudden, jarring noise. In the months that followed, the event refused to settle into ordinary recollection. Instead of a distant account, the scene played in his mind with hyper-real clarity—the exact pressure of the officer’s forearm, the metallic taste of his fear, the way streetlights reflected off the windshield. He would close his eyes and feel the same paralyzing terror he had experienced at the wheel, while simultaneously insisting to himself the story felt unreal, certain such an extreme violation could not logically belong to his previously unremarkable life. The memory’s intensity anchored a new, relentless vigilance. This shattered baseline dictated his professional reality. As an airline pilot, Tane found that ordinary physical closeness transformed into a palpable danger. When ground crew approached his flight deck door during pre-flight checks, the sheer proximity instantly triggered a conviction that an attack was underway. The fear of strangers moving toward him did not merely coexist with the past; it acted as a direct catalyst, pulling the fragmented police encounter back into sharp focus. Each time the memory intruded, it was accompanied by a violent startle response to the chirp of headsets or the thud of boarding stairs, cementing the trigger in his daily routine. His avoidance strategies formed gradually. When ground control held his aircraft on the tarmac, Tane’s throat would constrict with sudden nausea, his mind fixating on the delay as absolute proof that something catastrophic was about to happen. To escape the sensation, he stopped inviting anyone into his car. Driving with others became unbearable, and the lingering assumption that any delay signaled imminent danger made him hyper-sensitive to physical proximity and bodily nausea. Each new spike of threat perception sharpened the memory’s edges, rendering the original police encounter more real than ordinary recollection. The pattern calcified. The consequences mounted steadily. His divorce had been sealed by years of mutual isolation, and his aviation career teetered as he began to dread the gate delays that now guaranteed a panic response. He finally sought help because the nausea had become uncontrollable during taxiing, and he recognized he was losing his wings. What he feared most was that the cycle would continue to amplify until he could no longer distinguish the past from the present. He hoped to reclaim the sky without the constant, terrifying echo of the man at his window.
